research_concepts: PNR (pick-and-roll ball handler) suppression/failure as defined by the project's H1-to-H2 suppression trigger
PULL_UP as a counter play type (counter = a different play type run after a trigger)
lift in PPP (or play-type share) for PULL_UP after a trigger relative to a baseline
league-wide consistency across units (share of units with lift>0, median lift)
methodological_questions: Is 'PNR fail' defined from the outcome (PPP drop), and how does that interact with regression to the mean?
What is lift exactly (PULL_UP PPP minus which baseline: own H1, own season mean, or other counters' PPP after the trigger)?
What is the unit (team, team-season, team-opponent matchup) and how many post-trigger PULL_UP possessions does each have?
Do the 70%-of-units and 2pp-median thresholds have adequate power and a sensible null?
How are confounding (score state, garbage time, lineups, fatigue, opponent), placebo/pseudo-trigger controls and multiple testing handled?
evidence_establishes: Nothing: retrieve_history returned zero records, so no historical evidence was available for this question.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether any earlier project work tested PULL_UP as a counter after PNR suppression
Which lift definitions, unit definitions, thresholds or trigger rules have previously worked or failed
Typical trigger frequency, post-trigger sample sizes, or the base rate of PULL_UP lift in this data
own_inferences: The glossary defines a suppression trigger as a sharp H1-to-H2 PPP drop on a play type under minimum-attempt rules. A trigger is therefore selected on the outcome, so post-trigger PNR PPP would regress upward, and any 'counter lift' measured relative to the triggered PNR is mechanically biased.

Because the trigger is only observable after H1, the exposure window is H2 possessions, so per-unit counts of post-trigger PULL_UP possessions are likely small and PPP on them is very noisy (one possession is 0-3 points). A sign-based criterion like 'lift>0 in >=70% of units' is fragile at that noise level, and its meaning depends strongly on the unit.

A positive lift versus a baseline does not show PULL_UP is a counter. A counter claim requires PULL_UP to beat both the alternative counters (DRIVE, SPOT_UP, CUT and so on) and a no-trigger or pseudo-trigger placebo. Pull-ups are also usually selected by shot-clock and late-game situations, which confound lift.

The thresholds (70%, 2pp) look arbitrary and have no stated null. With 30 team units, P(>=21 positive | p=0.5) is about 2%, but the sign share can be pushed above or below 70% by unequal unit sizes alone.

The question may be too vaguely specified to run as posed. It becomes testable only after fixing lift, unit and baseline in advance, with the likely choice being team-season units pooled over 2022-23 to 2024-25 and held-out 2025-26.
uncertainties: Exact definitions of 'PNR fail' and 'lift' in the question are not given and were not retrievable
The data_catalog was not consulted, so field availability (for example a possession-level play-type label with clock and score) is assumed from the task statement
The number of triggers per team-season and the post-trigger PULL_UP possession counts are unknown
Whether BEST/AVOID app rankings already encode PULL_UP and could introduce circularity is unknown
The 2025-26 playoff data is partial before 2026-06-21, so the question date (2026-05-23) leaves it incomplete

historical_effect.explanation: Retrieval returned no records, so the decision rests on the task statement, the glossary and general methodological reasoning. The conclusion is provisional and no prior failed approach could be avoided or reused.

blocking_constraints.text: The PNR fail (trigger) is defined from an H1-to-H2 PPP drop, so conditioning on it selects on the outcome and induces regression to the mean in the post-trigger comparison.
Post-trigger PULL_UP possessions per unit are probably few, making unit-level lift signs close to coin flips unless units are pooled to team-seasons or larger.
Lift is undefined without a baseline PULL_UP PPP and share. Pull-up PPP is typically lower than other play types, and the question does not state a comparison.

prior_work.summary: No earlier work was retrieved. Whether this specific question was studied before is unknown.

risks.text: The trigger (PNR fail) is defined by low PNR PPP in H2. Using it to define exposure ties the exposure to the outcome and favors apparent rebound in whatever play type follows.
Triggers are selected on extreme H1-to-H2 drops, so the next possessions regress toward the mean regardless of the counter chosen. Lift versus the triggered PNR is inflated.
PPP is bounded and discrete. If the baseline is a depressed PNR PPP, nearly any alternative play type shows positive lift, so PULL_UP lift>0 would be near-guaranteed and uninformative.
Per-unit post-trigger PULL_UP counts are small, so noise dominates the sign share and the median lift of 2pp. Only 30 teams per season gives low power at team level.
Triggers need minimum-attempt rules and occur in a minority of games, and the later part of H2 is often garbage time, which further shrinks usable data.
Score state, lineups and substitutions, opponent defensive scheme, shot clock, fatigue and player quality (who takes the pull-up) all affect both the choice of PULL_UP and its efficiency.

The result depends on a credible placebo: pseudo-triggers in non-suppressed games or random half-splits, and the same lift for other counters. Without it, a positive lift cannot be called a counter effect.
If PULL_UP is one of several play types tested as counters, or if several unit definitions and thresholds are tried, false positives rise.
The rule-based classifier infers PNR from play-by-play text, so PNR and PULL_UP labels and the trigger itself may be misclassified, with different error rates across teams, seasons and venues.
Play-type frequencies and scoring environments differ across 2022-23 to 2025-26 and between regular season and playoffs, so pooling without season and context adjustment can mislead.

design.estimand: Difference in PPP (and secondarily play-type share) on PULL_UP possessions after a PNR suppression trigger versus (a) the same team's PULL_UP PPP in matched non-trigger games at the same game time and score state, and (b) the post-trigger PPP of each alternative counter play type (DRIVE, SPOT_UP, CUT and so on). 'Real counter' means PULL_UP exceeds both, not merely exceeds a PNR baseline.
design.unit: Team-season, with regular season and playoffs analysed separately. Teams with fewer than a pre-set minimum of post-trigger PULL_UP possessions (set from the empirical distribution before outcomes are looked at) are excluded and the number reported. A team-opponent unit is exploratory only.
design.sample: Confirmatory: 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular seasons, excluding garbage time and using the project's fixed trigger rule defined from H1 versus H2 with minimum-attempt rules. Holdout: 2025-26 regular season, complete from 2026-04-13, frozen and analysed once. Playoffs are exploratory because of small samples and the partial 2025-26 data.
design.power: Before analysis, simulate the sign-share and median-lift criteria using empirical per-unit possession counts and the observed PPP variance, and report power to detect a true lift of 2pp and the false-positive rate under a null with the same noise. A binomial test against 50% (not 70%) should be preregistered alongside a bootstrap CI on the median across units. If simulated power for the true 2pp effect is below about 0.8, report the result as underpowered, not rejected.
design.controls: Define lift against pseudo-trigger baselines to remove regression to the mean (the same team, play type and game structure with a random or matched H1-to-H2 split, or triggers on non-suppressed play types). Adjust for score margin, period and clock, opponent, lineup and player (shooter quality via player random effects), and shot clock where available. Use cross-fitting: derive the trigger on one half of the games and measure counter outcomes only on later possessions, with the same-possession outcome excluded.
design.falsification: The claim fails if PULL_UP lift is no larger than placebo-trigger lift, if other play types show equal lift (so lift is generic rebound), if lift disappears after RTM adjustment, or if sign share is below the threshold in the 2025-26 holdout. A negative-control play type with no plausible counter role must show about zero lift.
design.multiplicity: A single primary hypothesis (PULL_UP) and one primary lift definition. All other play types and unit definitions are secondary and corrected with Holm or FDR control, and the number of alternative definitions tried is logged.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if, in the confirmatory seasons and again in the 2025-26 holdout, (i) at least 70% of eligible team-season units have positive placebo-adjusted lift, (ii) the median lift exceeds 2pp with a bootstrap CI excluding 0, and (iii) PULL_UP lift exceeds the best alternative counter after correction. Rejected if the CI upper bound for the median is below 2pp with adequate power. Otherwise inconclusive. No threshold is changed after viewing data.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API play-by-play, rotation, starters, matchup and box-score files, and the derived play-type possession records, for 2022-23 to 2025-26 as of 2026-05-23. Freeze the classifier version and trigger rules, hash the possession table, record the 2025-26 snapshot date, and exclude playoffs until complete from 2026-06-21 for any confirmatory use.

methodological_questions: How should a PNR fail be defined without using the outcome?
How is lift in points per possession or efficiency defined and measured against a baseline for PULL_UP?
What is the unit of analysis (team, player, team-season) and how many units have sufficient sample?
Does a >=70% sign-consistency and median lift >2pp threshold have adequate power and avoid mechanical or selection effects?
How do we handle regression to the mean, selection, confounding by player quality and defense type, and multiple testing?
args.query: Prior studies on whether PULL_UP is a league-wide counter after PNR failure, with lift measured across units, thresholds of 70% of units positive and median lift above 2 percentage points

You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

TOOL_RESULT glossary:
# Terminology used in the research questions

This glossary is given identically in every condition. It defines terms only and reports no results. Definitions follow the published papers (Structural Influence; Detecting Defensive Suppression) where they exist.

- **Possession, PPP:** a team's continuous spell with the ball; PPP is points per possession.
- **H1, H2:** first half (periods 1 and 2) and second half (periods 3 and 4) of a game. RS and PO: regular season and playoffs.
- **Play type:** the label assigned to each possession by the project's rule-based classifier from play-by-play events. Labels include PNR (pick-and-roll ball handler), DRIVE, CUT, SPOT_UP, PULL_UP, POST_UP, PUTBACK and TRANSITION. A play-type mix is a team's share of possessions in each play type.
- **Initiator, initiation:** the offensive player whose action starts the possession's play type (for example the cutter on a cut, the ball handler on a pick-and-roll). Initiation records are possession-level rows linking initiator, play type and points.
- **Inferrer:** the classifier step that infers a play type (for example a pick-and-roll) from play-by-play text when it is not recorded directly.
- **Suppression trigger:** a team, play type and game in which the team's PPP on that play type falls sharply from H1 to H2 under fixed minimum-attempt rules; read as the defense possibly taking the action away.
- **Continuation, counter:** after a trigger, continuation means the offense keeps running the triggered play type; a counter is a different play type run instead.
- **BEST, AVOID (counter tiers):** the strategy app's matchup-ranked counter recommendations after a trigger. BEST is the top-ranked counter play type for that matchup, AVOID the lowest-ranked.
- **Structural fingerprint:** a team's standardized pattern of how play types share initiators.
- **Structural influence (load, L):** how much a team's structural fingerprint changes when one player's initiations are removed. L_pre is that quantity measured from games before an absence.
- **Usage:** a player's share of team possessions he initiates or finishes.
- **Role categories (Structural Influence paper):** by crossing usage (above or below the rotation median) with residual influence (structural influence beyond what usage predicts): Primary Organizer (high usage, positive residual), Shaper (low usage, positive residual), Terminal Scorer (high usage, residual at or below zero), Role Occupant or Specialist (low usage, residual at or below zero).
- **Connector:** a structural-role label used in later studies for players whose presence links teammates' play types; the exact rule varied between studies.
- **Hub:** a high-structural-influence player around whom a team's initiations are organized.
- **Absence spell:** a run of consecutive games a player misses (the main studies used at least 15).
- **Displacement (D_real):** how far teammates' play-type mix moves during an absence spell relative to before it (one minus the cosine similarity of the two mixes).
- **Mover, decoy:** a mover is a player who changed teams between seasons; decoys are comparison players used as placebo matches for a mover.
- **Stint:** an interval of play with the same ten players on the court.
- **Garbage time:** late-game possessions with a lopsided score, usually excluded.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether to make one more data_catalog call, since it would help but isn't essential, and I'm leaning toward finalizing now with caveats. I'm also defining the terms: the trigger is the PNR suppression drop from H1 to H2 in PPP, the counter is a PULL_UP run instead, and I'm still working out whether the lift should be PULL_UP PPP or the post-trigger share minus baseline.

I'm now working through the risks in the design: regression to the mean, since triggers are picked on a sharp H1-to-H2 drop, and whether the lift is defined against the team's own H1 PULL_UP PPP. I'm also checking the sample sizes per unit, the arbitrary 70% threshold against a sign test, and confounders like garbage time, fatigue, and scheme changes, plus whether conditioning on an outcome-derived trigger biases the result.

I'm checking whether a mechanical floor could make the lift look positive even without a real counter effect, and I'm also weighing placebo checks built from random or non-trigger games. My working estimates put the chance the effect is real at about 0.2, the chance it's an artifact at 0.3, and the chance the question is testable at 0.55, so I'm leaning toward proceeding with changes. There's no historical evidence to draw on either.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether to make one more data_catalog call, since it would help but isn't essential, and I'm leaning toward finalizing now with caveats. I'm also defining the terms: the trigger is the PNR suppression drop from H1 to H2 in PPP, the counter is a PULL_UP run instead, and I'm still working out whether the lift should be PULL_UP PPP or the post-trigger share minus baseline.

I'm now working through the risks in the design: regression to the mean, since triggers are picked on a sharp H1-to-H2 drop, and whether the lift is defined against the team's own H1 PULL_UP PPP. I'm also checking the sample sizes per unit, the arbitrary 70% threshold against a sign test, and confounders like garbage time, fatigue, and scheme changes, plus whether conditioning on an outcome-derived trigger biases the result.

I'm checking whether a mechanical floor could make the lift look positive even without a real counter effect, and I'm also weighing placebo checks built from random or non-trigger games. My working estimates put the chance the effect is real at about 0.2, the chance it's an artifact at 0.3, and the chance the question is testable at 0.55, so I'm leaning toward proceeding with changes. There's no historical evidence to draw on either.
